title: Building a Chat App
subtitle: From 2 friends to 2 million users
description: Follow the journey of a simple chat app as it grows from a weekend project to a platform serving millions. Along the way, you'll discover why systems break at scale — and the elegant solutions engineers have invented to fix them.

stages.title: Just You and a Friend

narrative.setup: You just built a chat app over the weekend. It's nothing fancy — a text box, a send button, and messages that appear on screen. You and your friend are the only users. Everything works perfectly.

blocks.content: Your chat app is live. You type a message, hit send, and your friend sees it. Even this simple app uses a structure every internet application shares: the [[glossary:client-server|client-server model]].

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the restaurant
blocks.content: Think of your app like a restaurant. **The client** (your browser) is the customer placing an order. **The server** is the kitchen receiving the order and sending back food. The customer never walks into the kitchen — they communicate through a waiter (the internet).

Here's how it works:

1. **[[node:client-1|Your browser]]** (the client) sends a message to [[node:server|the server]]
2. [[node:server|The server]] receives it and sends it to [[node:client-2|your friend's browser]]
3. Your friend's browser displays the message

One client, one server, two happy users.

blocks.caption: Your app right now — simple as it gets

blocks.content: Every app you've ever used — Instagram, Slack, Uber — started with this same pattern: a client talks to a server. The difference is what happens when millions of clients show up at once.
One thing to notice: your [[node:server|server]] keeps all messages **in memory** — like writing notes on a whiteboard. Fast and easy, but temporary.

blocks.question: What happens to your chat messages if the server restarts?

options.explanation: Data in memory is temporary — it vanishes when the server stops. This will become a real problem very soon...
Not yet! Messages only exist in the server's RAM, which is wiped on restart. We'll need something more permanent.

options.text: They're stored in the user's browser
options.explanation: The browser only displays messages — it doesn't store history. On refresh, it asks the server, and if the server forgot them... they're gone.

suggestedQuestions: What exactly is a server? Is it a physical computer somewhere?
Why can't both people just connect directly without a server?
What does 'in memory' mean in simple terms?

stages.title: 100 Friends Join

narrative.setup: You shared your app on social media. A hundred friends and friends-of-friends signed up overnight. People are creating group chats, sharing memes, making plans.
narrative.problem: Then someone reports a bug: 'I sent a message last night but it's gone this morning.' You check — the server restarted overnight, and every single message was lost.
narrative.resolution: You need a database — a permanent home for your data that survives server restarts.

blocks.content: Your [[node:server|server]] restarted overnight, and **every message disappeared**. A hundred users woke up to empty chat rooms.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: whiteboard vs. filing cabinet
blocks.content: Storing data in memory is like writing notes on a whiteboard — great for quick access, but if someone erases it, everything is lost. A **database** is like a filing cabinet: permanent storage that survives restarts, crashes, and updates.

The fix is a [[glossary:database|database]] — storage on disk, not just in memory.

1. User sends a message → server receives it
2. [[node:server|Server]] **writes the message to the [[node:database|database]]**
3. Server sends the message to other users in the chat
4. When someone opens the app, the server **reads messages from the database**

No more disappearing messages.

blocks.caption: Adding a database — your messages now survive restarts

blocks.content:
The most popular type for structured data like messages is a [[glossary:relational-database|relational database]] (like PostgreSQL). It stores data in tables — think spreadsheets:

| id | chat_room | sender | message | sent_at |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | general | alice | hey everyone! | 2024-01-15 9:00am |
| 2 | general | bob | hello! | 2024-01-15 9:01am |
| 3 | random | charlie | check this out | 2024-01-15 9:02am |
The database is a **separate system** from your server. This is a fundamental pattern: **separate compute (server) from storage (database)**. If your server crashes, your data is safe.

blocks.scenario: Users in the 'general' chat room complain that loading history takes 5+ seconds. The room has 50,000 messages, and your server fetches ALL of them every time someone opens the room.
blocks.question: What's the smartest first fix?

options.text: Only load the last 50 messages, then load more as the user scrolls up
options.explanation: This is called **pagination** — loading data in small chunks instead of all at once. It's the same pattern behind infinite scroll on Twitter/X or page numbers on Google.

options.text: Buy a faster, more powerful server
options.explanation: **Vertical scaling** (beefier hardware) works up to a point, but it won't help much when the real problem is requesting too much data at once.

options.text: Delete old messages to keep the database small
options.explanation: Users don't love having their messages deleted! This might work for ephemeral content (like Snapchat), but chat apps need history.

blocks.label: Deep dive: how does a database store data on disk?
blocks.content:
When you write a message to a database like PostgreSQL:

1. The message arrives at the database server
2. It's first written to a **write-ahead log** (WAL) — a sequential record that ensures no data is lost even if the power goes out mid-write
3. Then it's organized into the table's **data file** on disk, indexed so it can be found quickly later

This is why databases are reliable — they're designed to survive crashes at any point in the write process.

suggestedQuestions: What's the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
How does the database find a specific message so quickly?
Should I use PostgreSQL or MySQL for my app?

stages.title: The Group Chat Explodes

narrative.setup: Your app hit 1,000 users. People love it. Group chats are active all day. But users are starting to complain about something new: messages feel 'laggy.' They send a message and it takes a few seconds before others see it.
narrative.problem: You discover the issue: your app checks for new messages by asking the server 'any new messages?' every 3 seconds. With 1,000 users all doing this simultaneously, your server is drowning in 'are we there yet?' requests — most of which get the answer 'nope, nothing new.'
narrative.resolution: You need to switch from polling to WebSockets — a technology that lets the server push messages to clients instantly, without them having to ask.

blocks.content:
Users are complaining: *"Why does it take so long for messages to appear?"*

Right now, your app uses [[glossary:polling|polling]] — each client asks the server *"Any new messages?"* every 3 seconds.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: checking for a package
blocks.content: **Polling** is like walking to your front door every 30 seconds to check: *"Is my package here yet?"* Most trips, there's nothing there. It's exhausting for you and for the delivery person who keeps answering the door.
With 1,000 users polling every 3 seconds, that's **~333 requests per second** just for checking — and most return nothing new. Your server is drowning in *"Are we there yet?"* requests.
The fix: [[glossary:websockets|WebSockets]]. Instead of constant asking, a WebSocket creates a **persistent, two-way connection** between client and [[node:server|server]].

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: phone call vs. texting
blocks.content: WebSockets are like a **phone call** instead of texting. With texting (polling), you send a message and wait for a reply each time. With a phone call (WebSocket), the line stays open and both sides can talk whenever they have something to say.

With WebSockets:

1. User opens the app → browser opens a persistent connection to the server
2. When someone sends a message, [[node:server|the server]] **pushes it instantly** to every connected client
3. No more asking. No more waiting. Messages appear instantly.

This is how Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp Web all work.

blocks.caption: WebSockets: persistent connections replace constant polling

blocks.scenario: You've switched to WebSockets and messages are instant. But when a user's internet drops for 30 seconds and reconnects, they're missing messages sent during the disconnect.
blocks.question: How would you handle this?

options.text: When reconnecting, fetch missed messages from the database using a timestamp
options.explanation: The standard approach. On reconnect, the client says *"Last message I saw was at 9:15:32 AM"* and the server sends everything after that. Real-time delivery via WebSockets, database as the reliable backup.

options.text: Just accept that some messages might be lost
options.explanation: For a chat app, losing messages is unacceptable. This might work for a live stock ticker, but not for conversations.

options.text: Keep the old polling system as a backup alongside WebSockets
options.explanation: Two systems doing the same job adds complexity. Simpler: use WebSockets for real-time and the database for catch-up. You already have both.

blocks.content: **The database isn't just for saving data — it's your safety net.** WebSockets handle fast, real-time delivery. The database handles reliability and history. Combining a fast-but-fragile system with a slow-but-reliable one is a pattern you'll see everywhere in system design.

blocks.label: Deep dive: how does a WebSocket connection actually work?
blocks.content:
A WebSocket starts as a regular HTTP request with a special header: *"I'd like to upgrade this to a WebSocket."*

If the server agrees, the connection is "upgraded" — instead of request-response-hangup, both sides can send data at any time.

1. Client sends: `GET /chat HTTP/1.1` with `Upgrade: websocket` header
2. Server responds: `101 Switching Protocols`
3. Both sides can now send frames (small data packets) whenever they want

The connection stays open until one side closes it, or the network drops.

suggestedQuestions: How many WebSocket connections can one server handle?
Is there a middle ground between polling and WebSockets?
How do apps like Discord handle millions of concurrent connections?
